interactive.title: The sliding valve
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. The main picture is a valve that steers oil to a cylinder. The valve is a row of three square boxes. Below the row sit two fixed ports, P from the pump and T to the tank. Above it sit two more, A and B, joined to the cylinder. The ports stay put while the row slides left and right under them. Each box draws what the valve's moving part joins in one position. Inside each box, arrows show which ports it joins. A short bar across a port's end means that port is blocked. The left box has two straight arrows, P up to A and B down to T. The right box has two crossed arrows, P to B and A to T. A centre picker sets the middle box. It has three choices. Closed blocks all four ports. P to T has a line joining P and T, and bars on A and B. Float blocks P and joins A, B and T. Solenoid -Y1 and a spring sit at the left end of the row. Solenoid -Y2 and a spring sit at the right end. The cylinder stands upright above the valve. Its rod points up, with a load on top. A goes to the piston side at the bottom. B goes to the rod side at the top. The rod comes out upward and goes back in downward. Below the valve, a pump draws oil from the tank and feeds P. A relief valve on the pump's line opens to the tank when the pressure beats its spring. The rule. Only the box in line with the ports joins them. Each solenoid brings in the box beside it. A line carrying flow is drawn bold with arrows. An idle line is pale. Tap -Y1 to energise it. It pushes the row over until the left box sits against the ports. P then joins A, so oil fills the piston side. B joins T, so the rod side empties. The rod comes out. Tap -Y2 and the right box comes in instead. It joins P to B and A to T, so the rod goes back in. Tap a solenoid again to switch it off. You can also drag the row by hand. When you let go with both solenoids off, the springs push the row back until the middle box sits against the ports. A line under the pump says what it is doing. It may be feeding the cylinder or unloading to the tank. Or it may be on load, with its oil going over the relief valve. Once the rod reaches the end of its travel, the pump's oil goes over the relief valve. This happens even though the solenoid is still on. With the middle box in place, the centre picker decides. Closed blocks every port, so the rod holds and the pump's oil goes over the relief valve. P to T sends the pump's oil back to the tank at low pressure, and the rod holds. Float blocks P and joins A and B to T. The load pushes the rod back in steadily, and the pump's oil goes over the relief valve. A Leaks switch sets what kind of valve you are looking at. It is Off or On. Off is the ideal valve the symbol stands for. A held rod stays exactly where it stopped. On is a real spool, which leaks a little between its ports. A held rod can creep back in under its load. Here the creep is sped up so you can see it. A small mark shows where the rod stopped, so you can see the creep. A row of six cards sits below the main picture. Each card is a smaller symbol with its name and one line on what it does. A 3/2 valve: two boxes and three ports, with P blocked and A open to T at rest, and P to A when operated. A 5/2 air valve: two boxes and five ports, numbered 1 for the supply, 2 and 4 for the working lines and 3 and 5 for the exhausts. A relief valve: one box whose arrow sits off the line. A spring holds it shut, and it opens to the tank when the pressure beats the spring. A reducing valve: one box whose arrow runs along the line. It is open at rest and closes as the pressure after it reaches its spring's setting. A check valve: a ball against a seat, letting flow one way only. A flow control: two curves pinching the line, which set how fast the oil flows. A slanted arrow shows it can be adjusted. Tap a card to open it. The picture starts with both solenoids off, the Closed centre, Leaks Off and the rod half out. At phone width, the solenoid buttons, the centre picker and the Leaks switch wrap onto two rows with no word split. The cards sit two to a row. Every label is at least 12 px and stays readable at 360 px. Screen by screen. Screen 1, show, One box per position: the valve as it opens. Words: "A valve that steers oil is drawn as a row of boxes. Each box is one position it can take. Only the box in line with the ports joins them. Each solenoid brings in the box beside it. Four ports and three boxes make this a 4/3 valve." The three boxes light in turn, then the four port letters. Then the label 4/3 appears beside the valve. Read: the three boxes in a row, the four ports P, T, A and B against the middle one, labelled 4/3. Still: the end of the sweep. Screen 2, do, typed, Count the positions: a lone valve of two boxes, with four ports, P, T, A and B, on the right-hand box and a spring at the right end. "How many positions does this valve have?" A typed answer: 2, a whole number. Slips: 4, "That is the ports, which are the lines on the box. Count the boxes for the positions."; 1, "That is the box in use now. The valve can take any of its boxes." Hint: "Each box is one position. Count the boxes." Why: two boxes make two positions. With four ports, its label is 4/2. An intermediate switch works the same way. Its links run straight through in one position and cross over in the other. After Check, each box rings in turn. Screen 3, show, Slide the boxes: the valve as it opens. Words: "Inside the valve, a grooved shaft called the spool slides in a fixed body. The row of boxes stands for it. The ports never move. Shifting the valve slides the row until another box sits against them. Energise -Y1 and the box beside it comes in. P joins A, B joins T, and the rod comes out." Then "Tap -Y1." Read: -Y1 energised, the left box against the ports, oil running from P to A and from B to T, and the rod coming out. Still: -Y1 on. Screen 4, do, Which box?: the valve as it opens, with -Y2 marked as energised and the row not yet moved. "-Y2 is energised. Where does the oil from P go now?" Choices: To A; To B (right); Straight to T. Hint on To A: "That is the left box, which -Y1 brings in. -Y2 brings in the box beside it." Hint on Straight to T: "That would need the middle box. Energising -Y2 slides the right box in." Why: -Y2 pushes the row over until the right box sits against the ports. Its crossed arrows join P to B and A to T, so the rod goes back in. After Check, the row slides and the rod goes back in. Screen 5, show, Springs bring it back: the valve as it opens. Words: "A zigzag at each end is a spring. With both solenoids off, the springs push the middle box back against the ports. So the sheet draws the valve with its middle box against the ports. A notched bar is a detent. It would hold the valve in whatever box you leave it." Then "Drag the row to one side and let go." Read: the row pushed back by the springs, the middle box against the ports, and both solenoids off. Still: the row back at the middle after a drag. Screen 6, do, Let go of the lever: two lever valves side by side, each of three boxes. One has a spring at each end. The other has a detent, a notched bar, instead. "You push both levers to the left box and let go. Which valve stays in the left box?" Choices: The one with zigzags at its ends; The one with the notched bar (right); Both of them. Hint on The one with zigzags at its ends: "A zigzag is a spring. It pushes the valve back to its middle box once you let go." Hint on Both of them: "Only one of them has springs. Look at what each has at its ends." Why: the springs push the first valve back to its middle box. The detent holds the second wherever it was left. It stays in the left box until someone moves the lever. After Check, the sprung valve slides back and the other stays. Screen 7, show, The middle box: the valve as it opens. Words: "The middle box decides what happens at rest. Closed blocks all four ports, so the rod holds. With a fixed pump, its oil then goes over the relief valve. Closed keeps full pressure at P, ready for other valves. P to T sends the oil back to the tank at low pressure. That spares the pump from pushing against the relief valve. Float lets the load move the rod." Then "Pick each centre." Read: the P to T centre in place, the rod holding and the pump unloading to the tank. Still: the centre on P to T. Screen 8, do, Read the centre: a lone middle box with no label: a line from P straight to T, and a short bar across the ends of A and B. "Both solenoids are off and the pump runs. What do the cylinder and the pump do?" Choices: The rod holds, and the pump unloads to the tank (right); The rod holds, and the pump's oil goes over the relief valve; The rod floats, and the pump unloads to the tank. Hint on the relief valve: "Look at P. Its line runs straight to T, so the oil has an easy way back." Hint on The rod floats: "A and B each end in a bar, so they are blocked. Blocked lines hold the rod." Why: the line joins P to T, so the pump's oil returns to the tank at low pressure. The bars block A and B. The oil in the cylinder has nowhere to go, so the rod holds. After Check, the full picture opens on the P to T centre. Screen 9, show, Held is not sealed: the valve as it opens, with a mark where the rod stopped. Words: "A closed box is drawn sealed. A real spool leaks a little between its ports. So a cylinder holding a load can creep. The symbol shows the ideal valve, not its leaks. Here the creep is sped up." Then "Switch Leaks on and watch the rod." Read: the Closed centre with the load on the rod, and the rod crept a little back in, below the mark where it stopped. Still: Leaks on, after a while. Screen 10, do, Will it hold?: a cylinder holding a load up, its valve on a Closed centre with both solenoids off. "The load must stay up all night. Does the closed centre make sure of that?" Choices: Yes, the box blocks every port; No, the spool leaks, so the load can creep down (right); Yes, as long as the pump keeps running. Hint on Yes, the box blocks every port: "The box is drawn sealed. A real spool leaks a little." Hint on the pump: "The box blocks P from A and B, so the pump is not what holds the load up." Why: the closed box blocks the ports on paper. In the real valve, oil leaks slowly past the spool, so the load can creep down. A load that must not move needs a valve that seats tightly, such as a check valve. It also needs a mechanical prop before anyone works under it. After Check, Leaks switches on and the rod creeps below its mark. Screen 11, show, The other valves: the row of cards. Words: "Other valves use the same boxes and marks. A 3/2 has three ports and two positions. A 5/2 for air has five ports. A relief valve opens to the tank when pressure beats its spring. A check valve lets flow one way only." Then "Tap each card." Read: six cards, each a symbol with its name and its job: 3/2, 5/2 with its ports numbered, relief, reducing, check and flow control. Still: all six cards open. Screen 12, do, mixed, Slide the 3/2: the 3/2 card, drawn larger, with solenoid -Y1 at its left end marked as energised, a spring at its right end, and the row not yet moved. At rest its right box blocks P and joins A to T. Its left box joins P to A. "-Y1 is energised. Where does the supply at P go?" Choices: To A (right); To T; Nowhere, it stays blocked. Hint on To T: "At rest A goes to T. Slide the other box in and read its arrow." Hint on Nowhere: "That is the box at rest. Energising -Y1 brings in the box beside it." Why: -Y1 brings in the box beside it, whose arrow joins P to A. Switch it off and the spring brings back the box that blocks P and empties A to T. After Check, the row slides. Screen 13, do, mixed, typed, Count the ports: a 5/2 air valve with no numbers, at rest: one line at the bottom middle, one line either side of it, and two lines on top. "How many ports does this valve have?" A typed answer: 5, a whole number. Slips: 2, "That is the positions, which are the boxes. Ports are the lines on the box in use."; 3, "Count the two lines on top as well. They go to the cylinder."; 4, "Count both outer lines at the bottom. This valve has an exhaust each side of the supply." Hint: "Count every line on the box in use, top and bottom." Why: one supply, two working lines and two exhausts make five ports. With two boxes, it is a 5/2 valve. After Check, the ports are numbered 1 to 5. Screen 14, do, mixed, Read the label: the valve from screen 2 again, two boxes with four ports, P, T, A and B, on the right-hand box, and no label. "Which label fits this valve?" Choices: 4/2 (right); 2/4. Hint on 2/4: "That puts the positions first. The label gives the ports first, then the positions." Why: it has four ports, P, T, A and B, and two boxes. The label gives the ports first, then the positions, so it is a 4/2 valve. After Check, the label 4/2 appears.
interactive.ignores: The creep is drawn much faster than a real one, so you can see it in a few seconds. The row snaps from box to box. A real spool passes through in-between states on the way. Some drawings show those with small extra boxes. The cylinder has no friction, and its load never changes. Real sheets carry many more centre conditions than these three. Pilot-operated valves add small pilot lines. A proportional valve can sit anywhere between its boxes. Valves like it are drawn with extra marks. This lesson does not show how each valve is built or how it is set.

explain.text:
A valve that steers oil or air is drawn as a row of boxes. Each box is one position the valve can take. The pipes meet the row at one box only. That box shows where the flow goes in the state the sheet is drawn in. The others show where it would go in their own positions.

Picture the row of boxes as the valve's moving part. Inside the valve, that part is usually a spool. A spool is a rod with grooves cut round it, and it slides in the valve's body. The ports are fixed to the body and never move. Slide the spool and its grooves join different ports. Each box draws what they join in one position. So shifting the valve slides the row until another box sits against the ports. Only that box joins them. An arrow in a box joins two ports. A short bar across a port's end blocks it. On a 4/3 valve, the 4 counts the ports and the 3 counts the positions. The four ports are P from the pump, T the return to the tank, and A and B to the cylinder.[^1] A solenoid brings in the box beside it. Solenoid -Y1 is drawn at the left end. Energise it, and the left box comes in. On a common layout, its arrows join P to A and B to T. A goes to the piston side. Pressure reaches the piston side while the rod side empties, so the rod comes out. Energise -Y2 at the right end, and the right box comes in. Its crossed arrows join P to B and A to T, so the rod goes back in. A valve like this sends the flow one way or the other. It is a [[directional control valve]].

Something must bring the valve back. A zigzag at each end is a spring. With both solenoids off, the springs push the middle box back against the ports. So the sheet shows the valve there, in its normal or neutral position, unless a set of sheets shows other phases.[^2] That is its drawn state, with nothing operating it. A detent works differently. It is a notched bar, and it holds the valve in whatever box it was left. The middle box sets what the plant does at rest. That choice is the valve's [[centre condition]]. A closed centre blocks all four ports, so the cylinder holds. With no other valve open, a fixed pump's oil then has nowhere to go but over the [[relief valve]]. That valve opens to the tank when the pressure beats its spring. A P to T centre joins the pump to the tank and blocks A and B. The pump unloads at low pressure, and the cylinder holds. A float centre blocks P and joins A, B and T, so a load can push the rod along.

The symbol is an ideal. A closed box is drawn sealed. A real spool leaks a little between its ports, so a cylinder holding a load can creep slowly. Other valves use the same boxes and marks. A 3/2 valve has three ports and two positions. A check valve is drawn as a ball against a seat, and it lets flow pass one way only. **To read a valve, slide the box its actuator brings in against the fixed ports. Only that box joins them, and its arrows show where the oil or air goes.**

analogy.text: You know this from an intermediate switch on a stair lighting circuit. It has four terminals and two positions. In one, the links run straight through. In the other, they cross over. The terminals never move. The switch only changes which links sit between them. A 4/2 valve's two boxes are those same two positions. One has straight arrows and the other crossed arrows.
analogy.breaks: An intermediate switch stays wherever you leave it, like a detent. It has no springs and no middle position. Each terminal is always linked to another, so it has nothing like a blocked port. An open contact truly breaks the circuit. A closed spool still leaks a little.

practice.text:
- A centred valve does not prove a load is safe. A closed centre still leaks, so a raised load can creep down. Lower the load or prop it mechanically. Then isolate and vent by the plant's procedure before you work on it.
- Count the boxes. That is the number of positions.
- Count the lines on the box in use. That is the number of ports. The label gives ports first, then positions, such as 4/3.
- Name the ports. P comes from the pump, T is the return to the tank, and A and B go to the cylinder. Air valve ports are often numbered instead. 1 is the supply, 2 and 4 are the working lines, and 3 and 5 are the exhausts.
- Read each end. The marks there say what moves the valve and what brings it back. They may be a solenoid tag such as -Y1, a lever, a pilot line, a spring or a detent.
- Read the box against the ports. That is the drawn state, usually with nothing operating the valve.
- For each actuator, slide the box it brings in against the ports. Then follow each arrow from port to port.

**Rule of thumb:** the box beside a solenoid or pilot is the box it brings in. A lever drawn at one end can bring in either outer box. Springs bring back the box at rest. On a spring-centred valve, that is the middle one.

**Worked example:** a valve has three boxes. Its left end has -Y1 and a spring, and its right end has -Y2 and a spring. Four ports meet its middle box. That box joins P to T and blocks A and B. Its left box has straight arrows, and its right box has crossed ones. A goes to the piston side. Four ports and three boxes make it a 4/3 valve. At rest, the springs centre it. The pump unloads to the tank. The cylinder holds, though it may creep. Energise -Y1 and the left box comes in. P joins A and B joins T, so oil fills the piston side and the rod comes out. Energise -Y2 and the right box comes in. Its crossed arrows join P to B and A to T, so the rod goes back in.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the ports as positions, so a 4/2 becomes a 2/4.
- Reading the box already against the ports after a solenoid is energised. Slide the box beside the solenoid in instead.
- Taking a detent for a spring, and expecting the valve to come back by itself.
- Trusting a closed centre to hold a load for ever.
- Forgetting the relief valve. With a closed centre and a fixed pump, the oil still has to go somewhere.

sources.quote: The '4 way' means it has 4 pipe connections, generally Pressure, Return, Port A and Port B. The 'two position' means that it has two switched positions i.e. it can sit in the A or B position.
